title: The Indian Act: Status, Administration, and Control
intro: The law that tried to replace self-rule. Questions 57-60 are answered in this lesson — your writing saves here.

terms.def: Government policy aimed at absorbing Aboriginal peoples into Euro-Canadian society, pursued most directly through the Indian Act.
The 1876 federal law that defined Indian status, created reserves and band councils, and installed Indian agents with sweeping powers.
The federal representative on each reserve who controlled council meetings, approved bylaws, managed finances, and could remove chiefs.

body: Assimilation was the goal and the Act was the tool. Status rules decided who counted as Indian, and the 1951 Indian register later listed every status person, with rules that stripped status through marriage and other provisions, hitting women hardest until Bill C-31 ended much of that discrimination in 1985.

On each reserve the Indian agent, usually a non-Aboriginal man living on site, controlled council proceedings, approved every bylaw, managed band money, advised members on their supposed powers, and could remove chiefs and councillors. Band councils therefore held no real authority: they administered Ottawa's decisions.

Status rules show the same control logic applied to identity itself. The register system decided who counted, marriage provisions stripped status with women hit hardest, and only Bill C-31 in 1985 ended much of that discrimination. Identity, like land and money, sat in Ottawa's hands.

Walk the full chain for questions 57-60: assimilation as goal, status as gate, agent as warden, council as shell. Each mechanism answers one question, and together they explain why the Act counts as the central instrument of colonization in this course.

example.title: See it in the questions
example.text: Questions 57-60 move from assimilation to status to the agent to the powerless council. Pair each answer with its mechanism: goal, definition, agent powers, then the hollow council.

check.prompt: Why did band councils have no real authority under the Indian Act?
check.sample: Sample response: the Indian agent controlled council proceedings, approved all bylaws, managed band finances, and could remove chiefs and councillors, leaving councils administrative only.

title: Responses, Resistance, and the 1951 Revisions
intro: From quiet refusal to open movement to rewritten law. Questions 61-64 are answered in this lesson — your writing saves here.

terms.def: The federal proposal to end distinct Indian status. First Nations rejected it almost unanimously, turning resistance into a political movement.
The Indian Act rewrite: secret-ballot voting, women's first votes, an end to involuntary enfranchisement, the Indian register, and lifted bans on fundraising and lawyers for claims.

body: Resistance went underground first: few bands adopted European-style government, and bands dodged or defied the Act where they could. Ottawa forced compliance by withholding funds, programs, and services from bands that broke its rules.

The 1969 White Paper lit the movement by proposing to erase distinct status, and First Nations nearly unanimously refused. Earlier, the 1951 revisions had already cracked the control system: secret ballots replaced open voting and bands electing leaders rose to 263, women voted for the first time, involuntary enfranchisement ended, the register was created, and the bans on raising claim money and hiring lawyers were lifted, reopening the road to cases like Calder.

Each 1951 change unblocked a specific control. Secret ballots broke agent-run open voting; women's votes doubled the electorate; ending involuntary enfranchisement stopped the slow legal erasure of status; the register made status visible and contestable; and fundraising plus lawyers meant claims could finally reach courtrooms. Five locks, five keys.

Underground refusal deserves its own note. Before open movements were safe, few bands adopted European-style government and many dodged or defied the Act quietly. Ottawa answered by withholding funds, programs, and services from rule-breakers, which is why later victories taste of endurance as much as argument.

example.title: See it in the questions
example.text: Questions 61-64 run refusal, forcing, revision. Answer 64 with the four 1951 changes above plus the register; each one loosened a specific control.

check.prompt: Why was 1951 a turning point even though life did not improve at once?
check.sample: Sample response: the revisions restored votes, ended forced enfranchisement, and unblocked legal action, so political organization and court challenges became possible again.

title: Changing Relationships: Policy, Councils, and Devolution
intro: Landmarks, returning customs, and today's band government. Block B evidence checkpoint.

terms.def: Since the 1970s, the transfer of program and service control from Ottawa to band councils, including 1988 powers to tax, lease land, and manage royalties.

body: Three landmarks frame the modern turn: the 1969 White Paper's near-unanimous rejection, the 1973 Calder case reopening land rights argument, and the 1988 changes giving councils tax, leasing, and royalty powers. After 1951, traditional customs re-emerged on most reserves, with ceremonies again anchoring political, social, cultural, and spiritual ties.

A caution before questions 65-68: the textbook's page 66 dating around residential schools conflicts with National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation records, so treat its system-wide closure claim as disputed and answer from the chapter's policy content. Tribal council roles need the textbook's exact account on pages 66-73, so answer question 68 with those pages open. Block B checkpoint: you should now be able to explain traditional governance, the Métis and Inuit roads, the Act's machinery, resistance, 1951, and devolution.

Tribal councils solve the small-band problem. Band governments pool resources for programs, services, and policy-making through councils that, unlike band councils, are not regulated under the Indian Act but registered as provincial societies with federal funding. They also reach where the Act never went: justice, public safety, and law enforcement initiatives, while reinforcing traditional systems of mutual support.

Alberta runs eight of them, from Athabasca to Treaty Seven Management, each bundling member nations for shared capacity. Traditional customs re-emerging on most reserves complete the picture: ceremonies anchoring political, social, cultural, and spiritual ties again, after decades when the Act suppressed them.

example.title: Answer with the page open
example.text: Questions 65-68 mix landmarks with council detail. Anchor 1969, 1973, and 1988 to White Paper, Calder, and tax powers, then take council roles straight from pages 66-73.

check.prompt: What is devolution, and what did it give band councils by 1988?
check.sample: Sample response: Ottawa's transfer of program control to bands, reaching authority to levy taxes, lease reserve land, and manage mineral and royalty money.
